title: THESIS DEFENSE: Building Spatial Representations for Marine Habitat Understanding with Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
description: THESIS DEFENSE: Building Spatial Representations for Marine Habitat Understanding with Autonomous Underwater Vehicles Abstract:  Underwater robotic systems are increasingly relied upon for scientific exploration, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection. These systems typically have limited spatial awareness and, as a result, limited autonomy, performing preplanned missions and requiring extensive additional resources for deployment. These limitations are most consequential in coral reefs, among the most biodiverse ecosystems on the planet and critically under threat from anthropogenic disturbances and climate change. Within coral reefs, the predominant method for observation remains human divers. To bridge this gap, we develop spatial representations that enable underwater robots to understand the world, both physically and semantically, a foundation for scalable, autonomous operation in challenging marine environments. First, we incorporate a physically grounded underwater image formation model within 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), a radiance field method for scene representation. Jointly estimating medium parameters and the true underlying color alongside geometry, we create an efficient scene representation that overcomes the challenges of degraded imaging through water. Next, we remove 3DGS’s need for precise camera poses and a sparse point cloud from structure-from-motion. Instead, motivated by the noisy, multimodal navigation sensor data already present on underwater vehicles, we develop an approach to synergistically integrate this rich prior with 3DGS. This enables building such spatial representations with improved trajectory estimation with less computational cost. Finally, geometric and photometric reconstruction alone does not convey ecosystem understanding. In coral reefs, fish abundance and diversity are important indicators of ecosystem health. Towards measuring this, we show how visual fish detection from an autonomous underwater vehicle survey can enable rapid discovery of biological hotspots aligning with rugosity, a classical proxy for reef biodiversity. We also introduce a dataset, grounded in ego-perspective, in-situ imagery representative of field surveys, to benchmark progress on detection, identification, and tracking of fish. Together, these contributions lay a foundation for scalable, autonomous operation in challenging marine environments.Thesis Advisors: Yogesh Girdhar, John LeonardThesis Committee:  Sara Beery, Vincent Sitzmann TBD August 4, 2026 PHD DEFENSE: SigmaOS: a Cloud OS with a Unified API for Serverless and Microservice Applications Ariel Szekely MIT Part Of Thesis Defense 11:00 A - 2:00 P Location 32-G882

title: THESIS DEFENSE: Continuous Tensor Abstraction and Its High-Performance Compilation
description: THESIS DEFENSE: Continuous Tensor Abstraction and Its High-Performance Compilation Abstract: Tensor programming has become a standard abstraction for expressing and optimizing dense and sparse computations. However, existing tensor systems are built around integer-indexed domains, which makes it difficult to express applications whose data and computation are defined over real-valued coordinates, such as point clouds, genomic intervals, and spatial queries. As a result, these workloads are scattered across fragmented libraries, each with its own hand-written kernels and data structures. This thesis introduces the continuous tensor abstraction, which extends tensor programming to real-valued domains. Under a piecewise-constant assumption, continuous tensors can be represented finitely, reduced over continuous regions, and compiled into executable code. On top of this abstraction, the thesis develops format-aware computation: a program rewrite that turns continuous tensor programs into dense tensor operations with the format information embedded in the expression, so that highly optimized dense compiler infrastructure can execute them efficiently on GPUs. Together, these contributions broaden tensor programming beyond integer-indexed arrays and bring continuous-domain applications into a unified framework. title: Instance-optimal estimation of L2-norm
description: Instance-optimal estimation of L2-norm Abstract: The $L_2$-norm, or collision norm, is a core entity in the analysis of distributions and probabilistic algorithms. Batu and Canonne (FOCS 2017) presented an extensive analysis of algorithmic aspects of the $L_2$-norm and its connection to uniformity testing. However, when it comes to estimating the $L_2$-norm itself, their algorithm is not always optimal compared to the instance-specific second-moment bounds, $O(1/(\varepsilon\|\mu\|_2) + t_\mu/\varepsilon^2)$, for $t_\mu = \|\mu\|_3^3 / \|\mu\|_2^4 - 1$, as stated by Batu (WoLA 2025, open problem session).In this paper, we present an unbiased $L_2$-estimation algorithm whose sample complexity matches the instance-specific second-moment analysis. Additionally, we show that $\Omega(1/(\varepsilon \|\mu\|_2) + t_\mu / \varepsilon^2)$ is indeed the per-instance lower bound for estimating the norm of a distribution $\mu$ by sampling (even for non-unbiased estimators).  TBD Recent Results in Graph Property Testing via the Container Method Cameron Seth University of Waterloo 2:00 P - 3:00 P Location 32-G575 Also seen in: MIT CSAIL Events

title: Recent Results in Graph Property Testing via the Container Method
description: Recent Results in Graph Property Testing via the Container Method Abstract: Recent work has shown that the graph container method is a useful tool for analyzing property testing algorithms for a number of classic properties including k-colorability, rho-clique and satisfiability. In this talk we will demonstrate that there is a deeper connection between the container method and graph property testing. For hereditary properties, we relate one-sided testability to the existence of a type of container lemma, and we obtain quantitative bounds in both directions. As applications, we obtain closure results for partition properties and new testing results for graph and digraph properties such as the dichromatic number.  TBD August 17, 2026 Diagnosing and Managing Performance in Data Systems Markos Markakis MIT CSAIL Part Of Thesis Defense 1:00 P - 2:00 P Location 32-G882
